Your lecturer, Mr. John Jennings, is a member of the IT Department with a teaching and research focus spanning Cloud Computing, AR/VR development in Unity, game design, and human factors. title: Lecture Notes
section: Why Do We Study Cloud Computing?
text:
Why Do We Study Cloud Computing?
Cloud computing has become the default operating model for modern IT — organisations of every size now build, scale, and secure their applications on platforms like AWS rather than in on-premises data centres. Understanding how to architect solutions well on these platforms is now a core professional skill, not a niche specialism.

Module Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

Analyse the main principles of cloud computing and how they are implemented by providers such as AWS.
Define a solution using architectural design principles derived from customer requirements.
Assess various cloud architectures and implementations in order to solve common infrastructure problems.
Implement a cloud-based architecture grounded in well-designed architectural principles.



Indicative Syllabus
The module is organised into five units, each addressing a different lens on cloud architecture:

Unit 1 — Public Cloud Architectures: global cloud infrastructure, and the compute, storage, networking, and managed services that form the building blocks of any AWS solution.
Unit 2 — Resilient Architectures: high availability and load-balancing strategies that keep systems running through failure.
Unit 3 — High-Performing Architectures: architectural design for performance, auto-scaling, automation, decoupling, web-scale media delivery, and content delivery networks (CDNs).
Unit 4 — Secure Applications and Architectures: the AWS shared responsibility model, users/groups/roles, IAM, authentication and authorisation, and bastion hosts.
Unit 5 — Cost-Optimised Architectures: revisiting high availability and load-balancing through the lens of cost efficiency.

This module’s content closely mirrors the skills validated by the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) exam. While this is not an exam preparation course, the overlap is substantial and intentional. The exam — and much of this module — validates your ability to:

Design secure, resilient, high-performing, and cost-optimised architectures.
Review existing solutions and identify opportunities for improvement.

If you decide to pursue the SAA-C03 certification after this module, you will already have a strong conceptual foundation.

TipSuggested Starting Point



You’ll get the most out of this material if you already have a working understanding of: general AWS Cloud concepts; distributed systems (independent computers that appear to users as a single coherent system, characterised by concurrency, the absence of a global clock, independent failure modes, and transparency); and multi-tier architecture (separating an application into presentation, application, and data tiers to improve scalability, flexibility, maintainability, security, and reusability). If any of these feel unfamiliar, it’s worth a quick refresher before we go further.


Course materials include student guides, instructional videos, guided and challenge-based hands-on labs, a capstone project, recorded demonstrations, and instructor-led activities. title: Lecture Notes
text:
The Café Business Case
To ground abstract architecture concepts in something tangible, the AWS Academy curriculum uses a running case study: Frank and Martha’s café and bakery. Frank and Martha opened the business in retirement, and over the course of the programme, a small cast of characters — staff and AWS consultants — help them use cloud computing to solve real business problems.

Frank — co-owner, a retired navy officer who enjoys baking, non-technical.
Martha — co-owner, a retired accountant comfortable with spreadsheets, non-technical.
Sofía — their daughter, a supply chain manager with some programming skills, future business administration student.
Nikhil — an employee with visual design skills and a growing interest in cloud computing.
Olivia — an AWS Solutions Architect specialising in databases and networking.
Faythe — a developer skilled in AWS APIs and cloud security.
Mateo — a systems administrator focused on automation, repeatable solutions, backups, and disaster recovery.

What makes this case study valuable is that the café’s technical architecture evolves over seven versions, each reflecting a realistic business trigger:

V1: A simple static website hosted on Amazon S3.
V2: Dynamic content and online ordering — a web application plus a database running on EC2.
V3: Web and database layers are separated; the database migrates to Amazon RDS in a private subnet.
V4: A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is introduced to create secure, isolated subnets.
V5: A load balancer, auto scaling, and multi-AZ deployment are added to handle high traffic and improve availability.
V6: AWS CloudFormation templates automate deployment across multiple regions.
V7: AWS Lambda functions connect to RDS to generate scheduled reports.

You’ll see this business case referenced repeatedly throughout the module — treat it as a running example of how “good enough for now” architecture matures into something genuinely well-architected.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
Roles in Cloud Computing
Cloud projects involve several overlapping but distinct roles, and understanding them helps you see where a “cloud architect” fits into a wider team:

IT Professional — a generalist who may manage applications and production environments, often highly technical and sometimes specialised (e.g. security, storage). Typical titles: IT administrator, systems administrator, network administrator.
IT Leader — leads IT teams, manages operations and budgets, and chooses technologies for the organisation. Often hands-on early in their career before moving into delegation. Typical titles: IT manager, IT director, IT supervisor.
Developer — writes, tests, and fixes code, working at the application level using APIs and SDKs, sometimes specialising in areas like security or storage. Typical titles: software developer, system architect, software development manager.
DevOps Engineer — builds infrastructure following cloud architect guidelines and continually improves deployment pipelines. Typical titles: DevOps engineer, build engineer, reliability engineer.
Cloud Architect — stays current with the technology landscape, helps select appropriate technologies, and provides documentation, processes, and tooling. The cloud architect enables developer innovation and resolves cross-cutting challenges around cost, performance, reliability, and security. Typical titles: cloud architect, systems engineer, systems analyst.


Introducing Cloud Architecting
Taking the perspective of a cloud architect means understanding the practice of applying cloud best practices to a solution that uses cloud services and features to meet an organisation’s technical needs and business use cases. A cloud architect needs to evaluate architectures against the AWS Well-Architected Framework and apply best practices when building solutions on AWS — always working backward from the business need to the architecture, not the other way around.
The role of a cloud architect can be broken into three broad activities:

Plan — set technical cloud strategy together with business leads, and analyse solutions against business needs and requirements.
Research — investigate cloud service specifications and workload requirements, review existing workload architectures, and design prototype solutions.
Build — design the transformation roadmap, including milestones, work streams, and owners, and manage the adoption and migration process.

Key takeaways: Cloud architecture is the practice of applying cloud characteristics to a solution that uses cloud services and features to meet an organisation’s technical needs and business use cases. AWS services allow you to create highly available, scalable, and reliable architectures, and cloud architects are ultimately responsible for managing an organisation’s cloud computing architecture.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
The AWS Well-Architected Framework
The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a guide that provides a consistent approach for evaluating cloud architectures and for implementing sound designs. It documents a set of foundational questions and best practices, developed by AWS after reviewing thousands of real customer architectures, organised into six pillars:

Operational Excellence
Run and monitor systems that deliver business value, continually improve supporting processes and procedures, and treat your entire workload — applications, infrastructure, policies, governance, and operations — as code. Treating operations as code lets you apply the same engineering discipline to your infrastructure that you apply to application code, maximising productivity and minimising error rates.


Security
Implement a strong identity foundation, maintain traceability of activity, apply security at every layer (not just the perimeter), and implement risk assessment and mitigation strategies. Protecting data in transit and at rest, and preparing for security events before they happen, are central to this pillar.


Reliability
Design systems that recover quickly from infrastructure or service disruptions, that dynamically acquire compute resources to meet demand, and that mitigate disruptions such as misconfigurations or transient network issues. This pillar directly addresses classic reliability problems: single points of failure, lack of automation, and lack of elasticity.


Performance Efficiency
Choose and maintain efficient resources, and maintain that efficiency as demand changes. “Democratise” advanced technologies by using managed vendor solutions where implementing something yourself would be prohibitively complex. Employ mechanical sympathy — use technologies with an understanding of how they actually operate, for example choosing a database or storage approach based on real data access patterns rather than familiarity.


Cost Optimization
Measure efficiency continuously, eliminate unneeded expense, and adopt the consumption model that fits your usage pattern — often paying only for what you use. Favour managed services where they can operate at cloud scale and offer a lower cost per transaction than a self-managed equivalent.


Sustainability
Establish sustainability goals, maximise utilisation of provisioned resources, choose efficient hardware and software, and reduce the downstream environmental impact of your workloads. This is a continuous effort focused on energy reduction and efficiency across every component of a workload — from programming language choice to right-sized infrastructure.


The AWS Well-Architected (WA) Tool
The AWS WA Tool is a free, self-service tool available in the AWS Management Console that reviews the state of your workloads against the latest AWS architectural best practices. You answer a structured set of questions across the pillars, and the tool delivers an action plan with step-by-step guidance for improvement. It gives you consistent, repeatable access to the same knowledge and best practices used by AWS’s own architects, helping you minimise failures and operational costs, dig into infrastructure and business processes, and feed architecture considerations into your organisation’s governance process.
Key takeaways: The Well-Architected Framework provides a consistent approach to evaluating cloud architectures and guidance for implementing designs, organised into six pillars, each with foundational questions to assess alignment with best practice. The AWS WA Tool operationalises this framework directly in the console.

title: Lecture Notes
section: Best Practices for Building Solutions on AWS
text:
Best Practices for Building Solutions on AWS
Beyond the Framework’s pillars, AWS Academy highlights a set of concrete, recurring best practices you’ll apply throughout this module:
Design trade-offs. Every architectural decision involves trade-offs — for example, trading consistency, durability, or storage space for lower latency and higher performance, or prioritising speed to market over cost for a new feature. Base these decisions on empirical data (load testing, benchmarking) rather than intuition, since trade-offs can add cost and complexity.
Implement scalability. Design every layer of your infrastructure to handle changes in demand. Tools like Amazon CloudWatch can detect when load crosses a defined threshold (e.g. sustained CPU utilisation) and trigger Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to launch new instances automatically — and scale back down when demand drops, so you’re not paying for idle capacity. This is far faster and more reliable than manual, reactive scaling.
Automate your environment. AWS provides monitoring and automation tools at virtually every layer. CloudWatch and EC2 Auto Scaling can detect unhealthy resources and automatically launch replacements, notify administrators, and log changes for tracking — removing the need for manual detection and intervention when something fails.
Use Infrastructure as Code (IaC). Provisioning infrastructure through code instead of manual processes lets you rapidly deploy identical environments, dramatically reduce configuration errors introduced by manual steps, and propagate changes consistently across every stack. IaC also makes it straightforward to roll back to a last-known-good configuration if something goes wrong.
Treat resources as disposable. Think of your infrastructure as software, not hardware. Automate the deployment of new resources with identical configurations, stop resources that are not in use, and test updates on new resources before replacing the old ones — this makes it far easier to respond to changing capacity needs and to upgrade safely.
Use loosely coupled components. Traditional architectures often chain tightly integrated servers together, so a failure in one component can cascade and cause the whole system to fail, and scaling requires reconfiguring every connected layer. Loose coupling uses managed intermediaries — load balancers and message queues — between layers, so the intermediary absorbs failures and scaling events automatically. If one application server fails behind a load balancer, traffic simply continues to be routed to the healthy servers.
Design services, not servers. EC2 offers great flexibility, but it shouldn’t automatically be your default choice for everything. Consider containers or serverless solutions where appropriate. Use message queues for inter-application communication, store static assets off-server in Amazon S3, and let managed services like AWS Lambda, Amazon SQS, Amazon DynamoDB, ELB, Amazon SES, or Amazon Cognito handle authentication and state rather than building it yourself.
Choose the right database solution. Match the technology to the workload rather than forcing a workload to fit a familiar technology. Consider read/write patterns, total storage requirements, typical object size and access pattern, durability and latency requirements, maximum concurrent users, the nature of your queries, and how strong your integrity controls need to be.
Avoid single points of failure (SPOFs). Assume everything will eventually fail, and design backward from that assumption. A single database server shared by multiple application servers is a classic SPOF — if it goes down, everything above it goes down too. A common mitigation is a standby replica that can take over automatically if the primary fails, which also reflects the “disposable resources” principle in action.
Optimise for cost. Continually ask whether your resources are the right size and type for the job, which metrics you should be monitoring, how to turn off unused resources, how frequently a resource is actually needed, and whether a managed service could replace a self-managed server. Cloud computing lets you trade fixed expense (hardware you own regardless of use) for variable expense (paying only for what you consume).
Use caching. Caching temporarily stores data in an intermediary location between the requester and permanent storage, reducing both latency and cost for repeated requests. A classic example is Amazon CloudFront placed in front of Amazon S3: the first request fetches from S3 and CloudFront caches a copy at a nearby edge location; every subsequent request is served from that edge location at lower latency and lower cost.
Secure your entire infrastructure. Security must be built into every layer, not just the outer perimeter. Use managed services, log access to resources, isolate parts of your infrastructure from each other (for example using EC2 security groups to limit blast radius), encrypt data in transit and at rest, enforce least-privilege access control, require multi-factor authentication (MFA), and automate deployments so security configuration stays consistent over time.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
AWS Global Infrastructure
The AWS Global Infrastructure underpins everything above: it spans over 100 Availability Zones across more than 30 geographic Regions, offering 200+ services from data centres around the world, so you can build highly available, scalable architectures physically close to your customers for lower latency.
Selecting Regions. A Region is a physical geographical area containing two or more Availability Zones, connected to the rest of AWS via a private global backbone network rather than the public internet. Regions are isolated from one another for fault tolerance — data is never automatically replicated across Regions; you are responsible for enabling and controlling any cross-Region replication your business needs require. Some newer Regions are disabled by default and must be explicitly enabled, and isolated Regions such as AWS GovCloud (US) exist to meet specific government regulatory requirements. Region choice should be driven by compliance obligations and network latency requirements.
Selecting Availability Zones. An Availability Zone (AZ) consists of one or more physically separate data centres, designed as an independent failure zone with its own power, cooling, and networking, and interconnected to other AZs in the same Region via high-speed private links. Because no data centre belongs to more than one AZ, and AZs sit in different flood risk zones and power grids, replicating across AZs is one of the most effective ways to build resiliency into a system that must survive a full AZ outage.
Using Local Zones. Local Zones extend a Region into places where no full Region exists, placing compute, storage, database, and other select services physically closer to large population or industry centres. They enable single-digit-millisecond latency for use cases like media production, real-time gaming, and machine learning, while still connecting back to the parent Region over a high-bandwidth, secure link and through the same APIs you already use.
The role of AWS data centres. Data centres are where data physically resides and processing actually happens — typically tens of thousands of servers per facility, all online and actively serving customers. AWS runs core applications in an N+1 configuration so that, in the rare event of a data centre failure, remaining capacity can absorb the load through automated failover. AWS also uses custom network equipment sourced from multiple original device manufacturers (ODMs) with a customised protocol stack.
AWS Points of Presence (PoPs). Edge locations are AWS facilities placed close to customers specifically to deliver content — via services like Amazon CloudFront, Route 53, and AWS Global Accelerator — with the lowest possible latency. Regional edge caches sit between the origin server and the edge locations, holding content that isn’t popular enough to justify a permanent place at the edge, further reducing latency and load on the origin.
Key takeaways: The AWS Global Infrastructure consists of Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations. Region choice is typically driven by compliance and latency; each AZ is physically isolated with redundant power, networking, and connectivity; and edge locations plus regional edge caches improve performance by caching content close to users.

The capstone project in the AWS Academy Cloud Architecting (ACA) curriculum is designed as the culminating experience that allows learners to demonstrate their mastery of AWS cloud concepts, architecture best practices, and hands-on implementation. It integrates knowledge gained from the entire course, covering topics such as networking, compute, storage, databases, security, monitoring, and automation.
In the capstone, students are typically presented with a real-world business problem that requires designing and deploying a secure, scalable, and cost-effective cloud solution. They must apply the AWS Well-Architected Framework, considering the five pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, and cost optimization. Learners design architecture diagrams, justify technology choices, and implement core services like Amazon EC2, S3, RDS, IAM, VPC, and CloudFormation for infrastructure as code.
The project emphasizes not only technical accuracy but also professional skills such as documentation, communication, and solution presentation. By completing the capstone, participants demonstrate their ability to translate business requirements into a working AWS architecture. This project is also an opportunity to build a portfolio piece, showcasing readiness for cloud-related roles. Ultimately, it reinforces problem-solving, critical thinking, and applied cloud architecture skills in a practical context.
Once given the assessment brief, you will be required to prepare an architectural diagram solution to the problem and then over 2 weeks you will have the opportunity to create and deploy your solution architecture to AWS.
This project is worth 30% of your module grade.

text:
Assignment Overview
You are required to deploy a 3-tier Task Manager web application to AWS Learner Lab with enterprise-grade availability, fault tolerance, and security. The application consists of:

Frontend Tier: React single-page application
Backend Tier: Spring Boot REST API
Database Tier: MySQL relational database

Your deployment must demonstrate understanding of high-availability architecture patterns, disaster recovery principles, and AWS security best practices.

title: Assessment 3
text:
Technical Requirements

1. Network Architecture (25 points)

VPC Configuration

Create a custom VPC with CIDR block (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16)
Deploy across at least 2 Availability Zones (AZs)
Implement proper subnet segmentation:

Public Subnets (2+ subnets, one per AZ): - Bastion host subnet - Application Load Balancer subnet - NAT Gateway subnet
Private Subnets (4+ subnets, one per AZ): - Backend application tier (EC2 instances) - Database tier (RDS instances)


Internet Connectivity

Internet Gateway for public subnet access
NAT Gateway in each AZ for private subnet outbound traffic
Proper route table configuration for all subnets

Deliverable: Network architecture diagram showing all subnets, AZs, gateways, and routing




2. Frontend Tier - Static Web Hosting (15 points)

Primary Hosting

Deploy React application to Amazon S3
Enable static website hosting
Configure S3 bucket policies for public read access



Content Delivery & High Availability

Create CloudFront distribution pointing to S3 bucket
Configure CloudFront with:

Custom error pages
HTTPS support (CloudFront default certificate acceptable)
Caching policies for optimal performance
Multiple origin support (optional: S3 bucket replication)


Deliverable: Publicly accessible CloudFront URL serving the application




3. Backend Tier - Application Servers (25 points)

EC2 Instance Configuration

Deploy minimum 2 EC2 instances running Spring Boot application
Instances must be in different Availability Zones
Use Auto Scaling Group (ASG) with:

Minimum capacity: 2 instances
Maximum capacity: 4 instances
Desired capacity: 2 instances
Health checks enabled (ELB health check type)
Launch template or configuration




Application Load Balancer (ALB)

Create an Application Load Balancer in public subnets
Configure:

Target Group with backend instances registered
Health check path: /api/tasks
Cross-zone load balancing enabled
Listener on port 80 (HTTP)
Sticky sessions (optional)




Auto Scaling Policies (Optional Bonus: +5 points)

Create scaling policies based on:

CPU utilization (e.g., scale out at >70%)
Request count per target
Custom metrics


Deliverable: ALB DNS name with functional API endpoints




4. Database Tier - RDS MySQL (20 points)

RDS Configuration

Deploy Amazon RDS MySQL instance with:

Multi-AZ deployment enabled (automatic failover)
Instance class: db.t3.micro or larger
Storage: 20GB minimum, with auto-scaling enabled
Automated backups enabled (retention: 7 days)
Encryption at rest enabled




High Availability Features

Multi-AZ deployment with synchronous replication
Automatic failover to standby instance
Read replica in different AZ (optional bonus: +5 points)



Database Configuration

Create database taskdb
Configure security group for MySQL port 3306
Allow inbound traffic only from backend security group
Configure connection pooling in Spring Boot application

Deliverable: RDS endpoint accessible from backend instances only




5. Security Implementation (25 points)

Bastion Host Architecture

Deploy bastion host (jump server) in public subnet
Use t2.micro instance with Amazon Linux 2023 or Ubuntu
Configure security group:

Inbound: SSH (port 22) from your IP only
Outbound: SSH to private subnet instances




SSH Access Pattern

Backend EC2 instances must be in private subnets only
SSH access to backend instances only through bastion host
Implement SSH agent forwarding or key distribution
Document SSH connection procedure



Security Groups
Create and configure security groups for:
Bastion Host SG: - Inbound: SSH (22) from your IP - Outbound: SSH (22) to Backend SG
ALB Security Group: - Inbound: HTTP (80) from 0.0.0.0/0 - Outbound: HTTP (8080) to Backend SG
Backend EC2 Security Group: - Inbound: SSH (22) from Bastion SG - Inbound: HTTP (8080) from ALB SG - Outbound: MySQL (3306) to RDS SG - Outbound: HTTPS (443) for internet access (via NAT)
RDS Security Group: - Inbound: MySQL (3306) from Backend SG only - No outbound rules needed


IAM Roles (Optional Bonus: +5 points)

Create IAM role for EC2 instances
Attach policies for CloudWatch, SSM, S3 access
Use Systems Manager Session Manager as alternative to SSH

Deliverable: Security group configuration document and SSH access demonstration




6. Application Configuration (10 points)

Backend Configuration
Update Spring Boot application.properties:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://RDS-ENDPOINT:3306/taskdb
server.port=8080
# Add connection pool configuration
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5


Frontend Configuration
Update React application to use ALB endpoint:
const [apiUrl, setApiUrl] = useState('http://YOUR-ALB-DNS/api');


Health Monitoring

Configure ALB health checks
Implement application health endpoint (bonus)
Set up CloudWatch alarms (bonus: +5 points)

Distributed systems
A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that appears to its users as a single coherent system. These computers, often referred to as nodes, work together to achieve a common goal, coordinating their activities by passing messages to one another.
The key characteristics of a distributed system include:

Concurrency: Multiple components operate simultaneously.
No Global Clock: Each component has its own clock, and there’s no single, synchronized global time.
Independent Failures: Components can fail independently without necessarily bringing down the entire system.
Transparency: Users perceive the system as a single entity, unaware of the underlying distribution of components.

Examples of distributed systems range from simple client-server applications to complex cloud computing platforms, peer-to-peer networks, and blockchain technologies. They are designed to offer advantages like scalability, fault tolerance, and increased performance by distributing workloads across multiple machines.
Multi-tier architectures
A multi-tier architecture, also known as an n-tier architecture, is a client-server architecture in which the presentation, application processing, and data management functions are logically separated. This separation allows for greater flexibility, scalability, and maintainability compared to a monolithic or two-tier architecture.
The most common multi-tier architecture is the three-tier architecture, which typically consists of:

Presentation Tier (Client Tier): This is the top-most level of the application, providing the user interface and communicating with the application tier. It can be a web browser, a desktop application, or a mobile app. Its primary function is to display information to the user and send user input to the next tier.
Application Tier (Logic Tier/Middle Tier): This tier contains the business logic and application processing. It acts as an intermediary between the presentation tier and the data tier, processing requests from the presentation tier, performing necessary computations, and interacting with the data tier to retrieve or store data. This tier often includes application servers, web servers, and message queues.
Data Tier (Database Tier): This is the lowest level, responsible for storing and managing the application’s data. It typically consists of database servers (relational or NoSQL) and data storage mechanisms. The application tier accesses this tier to perform CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations on the data.

The benefits of a multi-tier architecture include:

Scalability: Each tier can be scaled independently based on demand. For example, if the application logic is heavily used, you can add more application servers without affecting the database.
Flexibility: Different technologies can be used for each tier, allowing developers to choose the best tools for specific tasks.
Maintainability: Changes in one tier have minimal impact on other tiers, simplifying development and maintenance.
Security: By separating the tiers, you can implement different security measures at each level, enhancing overall system security.
Reusability: Components within each tier can often be reused across different applications.

text:
Pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework

Pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework
The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a guide that provides a consistent approach to evaluate cloud architectures. It also provides guidance to help implement designs. It documents a set of foundational questions and best practices you can use to understand if a specific architecture aligns well with cloud best practices. AWS developed this framework after reviewing thousands of customer architectures on AWS.
The AWS Well-Architected Framework is organized into six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
You revisit the pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework in each of the modules of this course.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Operational Excellence pillar

Run and monitor systems that deliver business value.
Continually improve supporting processes and procedures.
View the entire workload as code.


The Operational Excellence pillar addresses the ability to run systems and gain insight into their operations to deliver business value. It also addresses the ability to continuously improve supporting processes and procedures.
When you design a workload for operations, you must be aware of how it will be deployed, updated, and operated. Implement engineering practices that align with defect reductions and quick, safe fixes. Make observation possible with logging, instrumentation, and business and technical metrics so you can gain insight into what is happening inside your architecture.
In AWS, you can view your entire workload (applications, infrastructure, policies, governance, and operations) as code. You can define and update all part of your workload using code. This means you can apply the same engineering discipline that you use for application code to every element of your stack. It is recommended that you invest in implementing operations activities as code to maximize productivity, minimize error rates, and set up automated responses.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Security pillar

Implement a strong identity foundation.
Maintain traceability.
Apply security at all layers.
Implement risk assessment and mitigation strategies.


The Security pillar addresses the ability to protect information, systems, and assets while delivering business value through risk assessments and mitigation strategies.
Your architecture will present a much stronger security presence if you implement a strong identity foundation, use and maintain traceability, apply security at all layers, automate security best practices, and protect data in transit and at rest. Implementing these security principles helps you prepare for security events.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Reliability pillar

Recover quickly.
Dynamically meet compute demand.
Mitigate disruptions.


The Reliability pillar addresses the ability of a system to recover from infrastructure or service disruptions and dynamically acquire computing resources to meet demand. It also addresses the ability of a system to mitigate disruptions, such as misconfigurations or transient network issues.
It can be difficult to ensure reliability in a traditional environment. Issues arise from single points of failure, lack of automation, and lack of elasticity. By applying the best practices outlined in the Reliability pillar, you can prevent many of these issues. The Reliability pillar helps you and your customers have a properly designed architecture with respect to high availability, fault tolerance, and overall redundancy.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Performance Efficiency pillar

Choose and maintain efficient resources.
Democratize advanced technologies.
Employ mechanical Sympathy.


When you consider performance, you want to maximize your performance by using computation resources efficiently. You also want to maintain that efficiency as the demand changes.
It is also important to democratize advanced technologies. In situations where technology is difficult to implement yourself, consider using a vendor. By implementing the technology for you, the vendor handles the complexity and the knowledge, freeing your team to focus on more value-added work.
Mechanical sympathy is when you use a tool or system with an understanding of how it operates best. Use the technology approach that aligns best to what you are trying to achieve. For example, consider data access patterns when you select database or storage approaches.

text:
Cost Optimization pillar

Measure efficiency.
Eliminate unneeded expense.
Adopt the right consumption model.
Consider using managed services


Cost optimization is an ongoing requirement of any good architectural design. The process is iterative, and it should be refined and improved throughout your production lifetime. Understanding how efficient your current architecture is in relation to your goals can remove unneeded expense.
Adopt the right consumption model for your use case. You might want to adopt a model where you pay only for the resources you use. Consider using managed services because they operate at cloud scale, and they can offer a lower cost per transaction or service.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Sustainability pillar

Establish sustainability goals.
Maximize utilization.
Choose efficient hardware and software.
Reduce downstream impact.


The Sustainability pillar addresses the ability to build architectures that maximize efficiency and reduce waste. The discipline of sustainability addresses the long-term environmental, economic, and societal impact of your business activities. You should understand the impact of your workloads and work to reduce the downstream impact. Sustainability in the cloud is a continuous effort. It focuses primarily on energy reduction and efficiency across all components of a workload by achieving the maximum benefit from the resources provisioned and minimizing the total resources required. This effort can include the initial selection of an efficient programming language, adoption of modern algorithms, and use of efficient data storage techniques. It can also include deploying to correctly sized and efficient compute infrastructure and minimizing requirements for high-powered end-user hardware.

Using the AWS WA Tool



Helps you review the state of your workloads and compares them to the latest AWS architectural best practices
Gives you access to knowledge and best practices used by AWS architects when you need it
Delivers an action plan with step-by-step guidance on how to build better workloads for the cloud
Provides a consistent process for you to review and measure your cloud architectures





Well Architected Tool




If you want help designing a well-architected solution, you can use the AWS Well-Architected Tool. The AWS WA Tool is a self-service tool that provides you with on-demand access to current AWS best practices. These best practices can help you build secure, high-performing, resilient, and efficient application infrastructure on AWS.
The AWS WA Tool helps you review the state of your workloads and compare them to the latest AWS architectural best practices. It gives you access to knowledge and best practices used by AWS architects when you need it.
The AWS WA Tool is available in the AWS Management Console. You define your workload and answer a series of questions in the areas of operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, and cost optimization. The AWS WA Tool then delivers an action plan with step-by-step guidance on how to improve your workload for the cloud.
The AWS WA Tool provides a consistent process for you to review and measure your cloud architectures. With the tool, you can gather data and get recommendations to do the following:

Minimize system failures and operational costs.
Dive deep into business and infrastructure processes.
Provide best practice guidance.
Deliver on the cloud computing value proposition.

You can use the results the tool provides to identify next steps for improvement, drive architectural decisions, and bring architecture considerations into your corporate governance process.

Key Takeaways

The AWS Well-Architected Framework provides a consistent approach to evaluate cloud architectures and guidance to help implement designs.
The AWS Well-Architected Framework is organized into six pillars.
Each pillar documents a set of foundational questions you can use to understand if a specific architecture aligns well with cloud best practices.
The AWS WA Tool helps you review the state of your workloads and compares them to the latest AWS architectural best practices.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Design trade-offs
As you design a solution, think carefully about trade-offs so you can select an optimal approach.

Evaluate trade-offs so you can select an optimal approach.
Examples of trade-offs include the following:

Trade consistency, durability, and space for time and latency to deliver higher performance.

For new features, prioritize speed to market over cost.


Base design decisions on empirical data.


As you design a solution, think carefully about trade-offs so you can select an optimal approach. For example, you might trade consistency, durability, and space for time and latency to deliver higher performance. Or you might prioritize speed to market over cost.
Trade-offs can increase the cost and complexity of your architecture, so your design decisions should be based on empirical data. For example, you might need to perform load testing to ensure that a measurable benefit is obtained in performance. Or you might need to perform benchmarking to achieve the most cost-optimal workload over time. When you evaluate performance-related improvements, consider how your architecture design choices will impact customers and workload efficiencies.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Implementing scalability






Ensure that your architecture can handle changes in demand.





Implement Scalability






When you run your workloads on the AWS Cloud, you can scale your infrastructure quickly and pro-actively. Make sure that you implement scalability at every layer of your infrastructure. By implementing scalability, you can improve your design to anticipate the need for more capacity and deliver it before it’s too late.
For example, you can use a monitoring solution like Amazon CloudWatch to detect whether the total load across your fleet of servers has reached a specified threshold. You can define this threshold to be Stayed above 60% CPU utilization for longer than 5 minutes or anything related to the use of resources. With CloudWatch, you can also design custom metrics based on specific applications that can invoke the resource scaling that is required.
When an alarm is invoked, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling immediately launches a new instance. That instance is then ready before capacity is reached, which provides a seamless experience for users.
Ideally, you should also design your system to be elastic. When demand drops off, you’re not running (and paying for) instances that you no longer need.
To understand the importance of scalability, consider where scaling is done reactively and manually. When application servers reach full capacity, users are prevented from accessing the application. Administrators then manually launch one or more new instances to manage the load. Unfortunately, it takes a few minutes for an instance to become available for use after it’s launched. That increases the time users can’t access the application.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Automating your environment






Automate the provisioning, termination, and configuration of resources.





Automation






AWS offers built-in monitoring and automation tools at virtually every layer of your infrastructure. Take advantage of these tools to ensure that your infrastructure can respond quickly to changes.
Without built-in monitoring and automation tools, you must manually detect and respond to any failures. If an application server fails, you must detect it and manually notify the administrator. The administrator must manually launch and configure the new server.
Tools like CloudWatch and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can detect unhealthy resources and automate the launch of replacement resources. You can also be notified when resource allocations change.
In this example, when the application server crashes, CloudWatch automatically detects the failure. CloudWatch automatically launches and configures a new servers and notifies the administrator. The change is logged to a change management solution for tracking.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Using IaC






Provision your computing infrastructure using code instead of manual processes.



Rapidly deploy duplicate environments.
Reduce configuration errors from manual configuration.
Propagate changes consistently to all stacks





Infrastructure as Code
Automation is a key goal across any computing environment. Infrastructure as code (IaC) is used for infrastructure automation to create environments. The most common use of IaC is in software development to build, test, and deploy applications.
Rapidly deploy duplicate environments. Using a single template, identical environments can be deployed. IaC removes the repetitive manual steps and check-lists that were needed in the past.
Reduce configuration errors from manual configuration. Manual configuration is error-prone because of human involvement. IaC reduces errors and streamlines error checking. If there are errors because of IaC code updates, you can quickly fix the situation by rolling the code-base to the last known stable configuration files. It’s also possible to roll back environments using previous versions of IaC configuration files for other reasons, such as the deployment of older application versions.
Propagate changes consistently to all stacks with IaC. Make a change to the template and push those changes to all stacks. This makes it possible for a change to be deployed consistently.
For more information, review What Is Infrastructure as Code? on the content resources page of your on-line course

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Treating resources as disposable






Take advantage of the dynamically provisioned nature of cloud computing.



Automate deployment of new resources with identical configurations.
Stop resources that are not in use.
Test updates on new resources, and then replace old resources with updated ones.






The best practice of treating resources as disposable refers to the idea of thinking about your infrastructure as software instead of hardware.
With hardware, you can buy more components than you need so that you are prepared for spikes in usage. However, doing this is expensive and inflexible—it’s difficult to upgrade because of the sunk cost.
Instead, when you treat your resources as disposable, migrating between instances or other discrete resources is fairly straightforward. You can quickly respond to changes in capacity needs, upgrade applications, and manage the underlying software.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Using loosely coupled components






Design architectures with independent components.







Traditional infrastructures have chains of tightly integrated servers, each with a specific purpose. The problem is that when one of those components or layers goes down, the disruption to the system can be fatal. It also impedes scaling. If you add or remove servers at one layer, you must also connect every server on each connecting layer.
With loose coupling, you use managed solutions as intermediaries between the layers of your system. With this design, the intermediary automatically handles both failures and the scaling of components or layers.
The example on the left shows a load balancer. Here, it’s an Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancer that routes requests between the web servers and the application servers. If one application server goes down, the load balancer will automatically start directing all traffic to the two healthy servers.
Two primary solutions for decoupling your components are load balancers and message queues.
The example on the right illustrates a collection of web and application servers that are tightly coupled. If one application server goes down, it will cause an error because the web servers try and fail to connect to it.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Designing services, not servers






Use the breadth of AWS services. Don’t limit your infrastructure to servers.



When appropriate, consider using containers or a serverless solution.
Message queues can handle communication between applications.
Static web assets can be stored off server, such as on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
User authentication and user state storage can be handled by managed AWS services






The next best practice is to design services, not servers. Although Amazon EC2 offers tremendous flexibility for designing and setting up your solution, it shouldn’t always be the first (or only) solution you use for every need. Sometimes, containers or a serverless solution might be more appropriate. Therefore, it’s important to consider what your needs are and which solution is appropriate.
With AWS serverless solutions and managed services, you don’t need to provision, configure, and manage an entire EC2 instance.
Managed solutions that have a lower profile and are more performant can replace server-based solutions at a lower cost. A few examples are AWS Lambda, Amazon SQS, Amazon DynamoDB, ELB, Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES), and Amazon Cognito.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Choosing the right database solution






Match technology to the workload, not the other way around.



Read and write needs
Total storage requirements
Typical object size and nature of access to these objects
Durability requirements
Latency requirements
Maximum concurrent users to support
Nature of queries
Required strength of integrity controls





It is important that you choose the right database solution. In traditional data centres and on-premises environments, limits on available hardware and licenses can constrain your choice of a data store solution. AWS recommends that you choose a data store based on your needs for your application environment.
For more information, see Choosing an AWS Database Service on the content resources page of your on-line course.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Avoiding single points of failure






Assume everything fails. Then, design backward.





Avoid single points of failure






Where possible, eliminate single points of failure from your architecture. This doesn’t mean you must always duplicate every component. Depending on your downtime service-level agreements (SLAs), you can use automated solutions that only launch components when needed. You can also use a managed service, so AWS automatically replaces malfunctioning underlying hardware for you.
If two application servers are connected to a single database server, the database server represents a single point of failure and should be avoided. When it goes down, the application servers also go down. Application servers should continue to function even if the underlying physical hardware fails, is removed, or is replaced.
A common way to avoid single points of failure is to create a secondary (standby) database server and replicate the data. This way, if the main database server goes offline, the secondary server can pick up the load.
In this example, when the main database goes offline, the application servers automatically send their requests to the secondary database. This example also exemplifies the best practice to treat resources as disposable, and design your applications to support changes in hardware.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Optimizing for cost






Take advantage of the flexibility of AWS to increase your cost efficiency.



Are my resources the right size and type for the job?
Which metrics should I monitor?
How do I turn off resources that are not in use?
How often will I need to use this resource?
Can I replace any of my servers with managed services?





With cloud computing, you can trade fixed expenses for variable expense. Fixed expenses are funds a company uses to acquire, upgrade, and maintain physical assets, such as property, industrial buildings, or equipment. Under this model, you pay for the servers in the data centre, whether they are active or not.
By contrast, AWS services use a variable expense cost model, which means you pay only for the individual services you need for as long as you use them. In each service, you can optimize for cost. Many services offer different pricing tiers, models, or configurations.
Remember, it can be very expensive to replicate an on-premises data centre setup of servers running 24/7 in the cloud. Therefore, the best way to build a cost effective infrastructure is to only provision the resources you need and stop services when they are not in use.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Using caching






Minimize redundant data retrieval operations, improving performance and cost.





Use caching






Caching is a technique to make future requests faster and reduce network throughput by temporarily storing data in an intermediary location between the requester and the permanent storage. The primary purpose of a cache is to increase the performance of data retrieval by reducing the need to access the underlying slower storage layer. Future requests for cached data are served faster than requests that access the data’s primary storage location. With caching, you can efficiently reuse previously retrieved or computed data.
In the example, the infrastructure uses Amazon CloudFront in front of Amazon S3 to provide caching. In this scenario, the initial request checks for the file in CloudFront. If it is not found, CloudFront requests the file from Amazon S3. CloudFront then stores a copy of the file at an edge location close to the user and sends a copy to the user who made the request.
Subsequent requests for the file are retrieved from the (now closer) edge location in CloudFront instead of Amazon S3. The second, third, and nth requests are at a lower latency and cost. After the first request, you no longer pay to transfer the file out of Amazon S3.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Securing your entire infrastructure






Build security into every layer of your infrastructure.



Use managed services.
Log access of resources.
Isolate parts of your infrastructure.
Encrypt data in transit and at rest.
Enforce access control granularly, using the principle of least privilege.
Use multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Automate your deployments to keep security consistent.





Security isn’t only about getting through the outer boundary of your infrastructure. It also involves ensuring that your individual environments and their components are secured from each other.
For example, in Amazon EC2, you can create security groups that you can use to determine which ports on your instances can send and receive traffic. Security groups can also determine where that traffic can come from or go to.
You can use security groups to reduce the probability that a security threat on one instance will spread to every other instance in your environment. You should take similar precautions with other services. Specific ways to implement this best practice are discussed throughout the course.
For more information, see AWS Cloud Security on the content resources page of your on-line course.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
AWS Global Infrastructure Topics

AWS Global Infrastructure
The AWS Global Cloud Infrastructure is a secure, extensive, and reliable cloud platform, offering more than 200 fully featured services from data centres globally. The AWS Cloud infrastructure spans 102 Availability Zones in 32 geographic regions around the world. This gives you the ability to launch highly available, scalable, and flexible architectures near your customers for lower latency and increased performance.
As you design and build architectures, you need to consider which region to deploy them. An AWS Region is a physical geographical location with two or more Availability Zones. Availability Zones, in turn, consist of one or more data centres. Your decisions should be based on the business requirements and the needs of the workload.
For example, if low latency is a requirement for your workload, you should consider using AWS points of presence (PoPs) or regional edge caches. The AWS PoP network sits at the edge of the network to reduce latency. Using these edge locations keeps your popular data close to your customers.
In this section, you learn about the AWS infrastructure, including Regions, availability zones, AWS Local Zones, AWS data centres, and AWS PoPs.
For more information about infrastructure on AWS, see AWS Global Infrastructure on the content resources page of your on-line course.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Selecting Regions



A Region is a geographical area.
Each Region usually consists of two or more Availability Zones.
Communication between Regions uses AWS backbone network infrastructure.
You enable and control data replication across Regions.





Regions




A Region is a physical geographical location with two or more Availability Zones. Availability Zones, in turn, consist of one or more data centres.
Regions are connected to multiple internet service providers (ISPs). Regions are also connected to a private global network backbone, which provides lower cost and more consistent cross-Region network latency when compared with the public internet.
Regions that were introduced before March 20, 2019, are enabled by default. Regions that were introduced after March 20, 2019—such as Asia Pacific (Hong Kong) and Middle East (Bahrain)—are disabled by default. You must enable these Regions before you can use them. You can use the AWS Management Console to enable or disable a Region.
Some Regions have restricted access. The isolated AWS GovCloud (US) Regions are designed to make it possible for US government agencies and customers to move sensitive workloads into the cloud by addressing their specific regulatory and compliance requirements.
To achieve fault tolerance and stability, Regions are isolated from one another. Resources in one Region are not automatically replicated to other Regions. When you store data in a specific Region, it is not replicated outside that Region. It is your responsibility to replicate data across Regions if your business needs require it. AWS provides information about the country and—where applicable—the state where each Region resides. You are responsible for selecting the Region where you should store data based on your compliance and network latency requirements.
AWS products and services are available by Region, so you might not have access to all Regions available for a given service.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Selecting Availability Zones



Each Availability Zone includes the following:

It is made up of one or more data centres.
It is designed for fault isolation.
It is interconnected with other Availability Zones in a Region using high-speed private links.

For certain services, you can choose your Availability Zones.
AWS recommends replicating across Availability Zones for resiliency.





Availability Zones



Each Region consists of two or more isolated locations that called Availability Zones. Each Availability Zone comprises one or more data centres, with some Availability Zones having as many as six data centres. However, no data centre can be a part of two Availability Zones.
Each Availability Zone is designed as an independent failure zone. This means that Availability Zones are physically separated in a typical metropolitan Region. They are also located in lower-risk floodplains (specific flood-zone categorization varies by Region). Availability Zones have a discrete, uninterruptible power supply and on-site backup generation facilities. In addition, they are each fed by different grids from independent utilities to further reduce single points of failure. Availability Zones are all redundantly connected to multiple tier-1 transit providers.
An Availability Zone is the most granular level of specification that you can make for certain services, such as Amazon EC2.
You are responsible for selecting the Availability Zones where your systems will reside. Systems can span multiple Availability Zones. You should design your systems to survive temporary or prolonged failure of an Availability Zone if a disaster occurs. Distributing applications across multiple Availability Zones means they can remain resilient in most failure situations, including natural disasters or system failures.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Using Local Zones

Local Zones make it possible for you to run latency-sensitive portions of applications closer to end users and resources in a specific geography.
They are an extension of a Region. With Local Zones, you can place AWS compute, storage, database, and other select services closer to large population, industry, and IT centres where no Regions exist today.
Local Zones are managed and supported by AWS.


Local Zones are a type of AWS infrastructure deployment. They place AWS compute, storage, database, and other select services closer to large population, industry, and IT centres where no Regions exist today. With Local Zones, you can run latency-sensitive portions of applications closer to end users and resources in a specific geography. You can use Local Zones to deliver single-digit millisecond latency for use cases such as media and entertainment content creation, real-time gaming, reservoir simulations, electronic design automation, and machine learning (ML).
Each Local Zone location is an extension of a Region. You can run latency-sensitive applications in a Local Zone by using AWS services such as Amazon EC2, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS), Amazon FSx, and ELB in geographic proximity to end users. Local Zones provide a high-bandwidth, secure connection between local workloads and workloads that run in the Region. With Local Zones you can seamlessly connect back to your other workloads that are running in AWS. You can connect to the full range of in-Region services through the same APIs and toolsets.
Local Zones are managed and supported by AWS, and they provide you with all the elasticity, scalability, and security benefits of the cloud. With Local Zones, you can build and deploy latency-sensitive applications closer to your end users by using a consistent set of AWS services. You can also scale up or scale down, and you pay only for the resources you use.
For more information, see AWS Local Zones on the content resources page of your on-line course.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Role of AWS data centers



Data centres are where the data resides and data processing occurs.
A data centre typically has tens of thousands of servers.
All data centres are on-line and serving customers.
AWS custom network equipment includes the following:

Is sourced from multiple ODMs
Has a customized network protocol stack






Data Centers




The foundation for the AWS infrastructure is the data centres. You do not specify a data centre for the deployment of resources. However, a data centre is the location where the actual data resides. Amazon operates state-of-the-art, highly available data centres. Though rare, failures that affect the availability of instances in the same location can occur. If you host all your instances in a single location that is affected by such a failure, none of your instances will be available.
All data centres are on-line and serving customers. In case of failure, automated processes move customer data traffic away from the affected area. Core applications are deployed in an N+1 configuration. In the event of a data centre failure, there is sufficient capacity for traffic to be load balanced to the remaining sites.
AWS uses custom network equipment sourced from multiple original device manufacturers (ODMs). ODMs design and manufacture products based on specifications from another company. The other company then re-brands the products for sale.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
AWS PoPs




Edge Location

AWS data centres and servers located close to customers and designed to deliver services with the lowest latency possible





Regional edge cache

AWS data centres between the origin server and the edge location that have a longer cache



To deliver content to end users with lower latency, CloudFront uses a global network that includes more than 410 PoPs. The PoPs are comprised of 400 edge locations and 13 regional mid-tier caches. These PoPs are the initial destination for a CloudFront request.
The edge locations make sure that popular content can be served quickly to customers. Regional edge caches bring more of your content closer to customers even if it is not popular enough to stay at an edge location. This helps reduce latency for customers. Regional edge caches increase efficiency and are transparent to the end user. Edge locations are located in North America, Europe, Asia, Australia, South America, the Middle East, Africa, and China. Edge locations support AWS services like Amazon Route 53, AWS Global Accelerator, and CloudFront.
Regional edge caches are used by default with CloudFront. They are used when you have content that is not accessed frequently enough to remain in an edge location. Regional edge caches absorb this content and provide an alternative to fetching the content from the origin server.
For more information, see Points of Presence on the content resources page of your on-line course.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Key Takeaways

The AWS Global Infrastructure consists of Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations.
Your choice of a Region is typically based on compliance requirements or to reduce latency.
Each Availability Zone is physically separate from other Availability Zones and has redundant power, networking, and connectivity.
Edge locations and regional edge caches improve performance by caching content closer to users.
